name: ChartQA
description: A large-scale benchmark for question answering about charts with visual and logical reasoning, covering 9,608 human-written questions and 23,111 machine-generated questions over real-world charts curated from four online sources.
creator: Ahmed Masry, Do Xuan Long, Jia Qing Tan, Shafiq Joty, Enamul Hoque
citeAs: Masry, Ahmed, Do Xuan Long, Jia Qing Tan, Shafiq Joty, and Enamul Hoque. 2022. ChartQA: A Benchmark for Question Answering about Charts with Visual and Logical Reasoning.
rai:dataCollection: The benchmark was constructed by crawling charts from four online sources: Statista, Pew Research, Our World In Data, and OECD, to ensure diversity in topics and visual styles. For Pew, only chart images were crawled because underlying data tables were unavailable. For the other three sources, the authors extracted underlying data tables, metadata such as title and chart type, SVG files, and associated text descriptions. Bounding box information for chart elements was extracted from SVG files to train data extraction models. The dataset includes two annotation procedures: collecting human-authored question-answer pairs using Amazon Mechanical Turk and generating question-answer pairs automatically from Statista human-written chart summaries using T5 models.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data, Software Collection
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: For the Pew dataset, only chart images were crawled since the underlying data tables are not available.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data sources include publicly available real-world charts from Statista, Pew Research, Our World In Data, and OECD. For Statista, OWID, and OECD, the collected raw materials included chart images, underlying data tables, metadata, SVG files, and text descriptions. For Pew, only chart images were collected.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The authors extracted bounding boxes of chart elements from SVG files to train data extraction models. They extended ChartOCR to extract fully structured data tables by recognizing chart text with CRAFT and associating data values with text labels using positional and color information. For machine-generated QA pairs, they filtered out invalid questions using a heuristic that removed questions whose answers could not be found in the chart data table, and they manually cleaned the test set by removing invalid questions.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For charts from Statista, OWID, and OECD, underlying data tables, metadata, SVG files, and text descriptions were extracted. Bounding boxes of chart elements were extracted from SVG files. For automatic question generation, a pre-trained T5 model fine-tuned on SQuAD was applied to human-written chart summaries to generate answers and answer-aware questions. Invalid generated questions were filtered out if the answer could not be found in the chart data table. The human-written and machine-generated QA pairs were then randomly split into train, validation, and test sets.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human-authored QA pairs were collected through Amazon Mechanical Turk. Workers were asked to focus on two types of questions for each chart image: compositional questions involving at least two mathematical or logical operations, and visual questions referring to visual attributes such as color, height, and length of graphical marks. For each chart, workers provided two questions with answers. The same questions were then answered by another annotator. If both workers' answers exactly matched, the answer was accepted as correct; otherwise, the authors manually checked the answers to select the final correct answer. In each HIT, workers verified two previously asked questions and also provided two new QA pairs. For machine-generated QA pairs, two T5 models were used: one for answer extraction from human-written Statista summaries and one for answer-aware question generation.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The agreement between crowdworkers based on exact matches was 61.04%. Because exact match does not account for typos or lexical variations, the authors manually checked agreement on 500 random samples and found agreement increased to 78.55% when considering typos and lexical variations. For machine-generated questions, after heuristic filtering, manual analysis of 1,250 QA pairs found that 86.64% were complete, answerable, and correct given the chart. The test set of the machine-generated dataset was manually cleaned by removing invalid questions.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Amazon Mechanical Turk workers with an acceptance rate of 95% and at least 5000 accomplished HITs; workers were further filtered using a pre-test. The paper also notes consideration of the minimum wage in the United States for compensation.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: T5 model fine-tuned on SQuAD for answer extraction and answer-aware question generation; CRAFT for text recognition; ChartOCR for chart data extraction
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset sources include charts about social and economic issues, demographic trends, public opinion, politics, health, economy, and society. The paper mentions topics such as demographic trends and public opinion, but does not specify sensitive attributes collected as dataset fields. Annotator data were anonymized.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors state that their models can be abused to mislead the public about chart content and implications. They also note that the benchmark is intended to help address challenges in answering visual and logical reasoning questions about charts.
rai:dataBiases: The paper notes that politics is a common topic among all sources and particularly dominant in the Pew dataset, where nearly half of charts are about U.S. Politics & Policy (45.4%). Bar charts are the most common chart type across the dataset. The machine-generated questions may include invalid questions due to mismatch between training and test domains.
rai:dataLimitations: The benchmark remains challenging, with lower accuracies than previous datasets. Machine-generated questions can be incomplete or unanswerable, requiring heuristic filtering and manual cleaning. Performance decreases when gold data tables are not provided, highlighting limitations of automatic chart data extraction on real-world charts with diverse styles. The models struggle with nested logical and arithmetic operations, complex visual compositional questions, and computer vision errors in data extraction. The authors also state they cannot guarantee model outputs will always be correct.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is presented as a benchmark for chart question answering with visual and logical reasoning. It is used for training, validation, and testing models under two settings: with gold data tables provided and with automatically extracted data tables. The benchmark is intended for evaluating transformer-based QA models and studying challenges in answering human-written visual and compositional questions about real-world charts.
